summary: This work studies distributed implementations of the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code across 4, 6, and 12 quantum processors connected via a star network using shared Bell pairs for nonlocal gates. The pseudo-threshold decreases monotonically from $p_0 \approx 0.0063$ (monolithic, $\alpha=1$) to $p_0 \approx 0.0016$–$0.0023$ as nonlocal gate error penalty $\alpha$ increases to 7, with coarser partitioning (4 QPU) outperforming finer ones ($\alpha \geq 3$).
motivation: Bivariate bicycle codes offer higher encoding rates than surface codes but require long-range stabilizer interactions difficult to implement on monolithic devices with nearest-neighbor connectivity. Modular architectures with all-to-all intra-QPU connectivity and entanglement-mediated inter-QPU gates are feasible on trapped-ion and neutral-atom platforms, but their noise characteristics require systematic analysis.
method: The authors partition the [[144,12,12]] BB code (12×6 torus, 144 qubits, 12 logical qubits) into contiguous vertical strips across QPUs, classify CNOT gates as local ($p$) or nonlocal ($\alpha p$), and perform Monte Carlo simulations with BP+OSD decoding under circuit-level depolarizing noise. They extend the BB code ansatz to $p_L(p,\alpha) = p^{d'_{\text{circ}}/2} \exp[c_0(\alpha) + c_1(\alpha)p + c_2(\alpha)p^2]$ with quadratic $\alpha$-dependence.
result: For 12 QPUs, pseudo-threshold decreases from $p_0(1)=0.006343$ to $p_0(7)=0.001651$ as $\alpha \in \{1,3,5,7\}$; similar trends hold for 6 and 4 QPU partitions with $p_0(7)$ values of 0.001912 and 0.002313 respectively. Fits achieve logarithmic $R^2 > 0.989$ across all configurations, confirming the ansatz captures distributed BB code degradation quantitatively.
